import SettingsPath from '@components/SettingsPath.astro';

A glass theme makes the keyboard's surfaces see-through, blurs what is behind them, and dresses each one with a rim of light and a little grain so a translucent key reads as a pane of frosted glass rather than as a colour you can see through. It is a per-theme setting: every custom theme carries its own **Glass** section in the [theme editor](/themes/editor/#glass), and the built-in **Frost** family shows the three ways it can be used.

<SettingsPath path="Appearance / Keyboard themes / (edit a theme) / Glass" />

## What is behind the glass

Glass blurs whatever is behind it, and a theme has three things it can put there.

**The app behind the keyboard.** With **Blur behind the keyboard** on, the keyboard asks Android to blur whatever app is under its window, and the board's own colour becomes a tint over that blur. This is the system's own window blur, the one the notification shade uses, so it costs the keyboard nothing per frame. It needs Android 12 or later, and it only runs while the phone allows window blur at all: battery saver turns it off, the developer option *Allow window-level blurs* turns it off, and some manufacturers never enable it on their cheaper models. The keyboard watches that state live.

Whenever the blur cannot run, the board stands on your wallpaper instead (see below), or, with nothing behind the glass, is drawn at least as opaque as the theme's **Board opacity without blur** slider says (92% by default). The keys of a glass theme were designed to sit on a blur, and over a sharp app at 40% they would be unreadable; the fallback keeps them readable and the theme still looks like itself. The floating keyboard never blurs behind itself either, because its window spans the whole screen and the blur would cover the whole app, so it uses the fallback too. Power saving (under Battery) switches the blur off as well.

**The theme's background image.** A theme with a [background image](/themes/backgrounds/) keeps that image sharp on the board, and the glass surfaces show it *blurred* where they cover it. The keyboard bakes one blurred, re-saturated copy of the image when the theme is applied, and every glass surface draws the slice of that copy that lies under it, then its own translucent colour on top. Nothing is blurred while you type: a key's face is one image draw with the right offset. This works on every Android version. The bake follows three sliders: **Backdrop blur**, **Backdrop saturation** and **Backdrop brightness**. The board's own **Image blur** is separate, so the board can be sharp while the keys are frosted, or both can be soft.

**Your wallpaper.** With no image of its own, a glass theme stands on a band of your wallpaper: the bottom of it by default, where the keyboard sits, or the middle or the top under **Part of the wallpaper**. The band is drawn as the board's own picture, under the board colour, and baked for the keys the same way an image is. That is what a window-blur theme falls back to where the app cannot be blurred (an older Android, battery saver, the floating keyboard, the editor's preview), so instead of going opaque the board shows your wallpaper blurred, which is close to what the blurred app would have looked like. The built-in **Frost wallpaper** look asks for the wallpaper outright and never blurs the app, so its backdrop is steady whatever you are typing into.

Whether that band is the wallpaper's real picture depends on the phone. Android 13 and later keep the wallpaper's pixels private from every app, so there the keyboard paints soft fields of light in the wallpaper's own three colours instead, which the system does publish; under the glass's blur the two read much the same. On Android 12 and below the picture itself can be read once the theme editor's **Use your real wallpaper** row has been allowed storage access; until then the colour fields stand in there too. A phone with no wallpaper colours at all (Android 8.0) gets the fields in the theme's own colours.

**Behind the glass** in the editor picks between these: **Auto** (the image if the theme has one, otherwise the wallpaper whenever the app is not being blurred), **Image**, **Wallpaper** (always, even where the app could be blurred instead) and **Nothing**.

A board with nothing behind its glass is simply its own see-through colour, with the rim and the grain. Over a gradient that already looks right, since blurring a smooth gradient changes nothing. An animated background image (a GIF or animated WebP) that is playing cannot be baked either; its glass surfaces are tint-only until the animation is stopped or reduce motion stills it.

## Which surfaces are glass

**Glass surfaces** is a row of chips, one per part of the keyboard: Letter keys, Modifier keys, Enter key, Space bar, Bars (the suggestion strip and every row stacked with it), Tool buttons, Chips, Cards, Popups (the press-and-hold alternates and the key-preview bubble) and Menus (the language picker and the clipboard, emoji and symbol menus). A fresh glass theme has every surface on except the Enter key, whose solid accent is what makes it easy to find.

Popups and menus are windows of their own, so they cannot sample the board's baked image. On Android 12 and later they ask the system to blur the keys under them instead, at the theme's **Blur strength**, which makes a popup over a glass board read as glass over glass. Where that is not available they are drawn at the fallback opacity, like the board.

## Rim and grain

Every glass surface gets a one-pixel **Rim**: a hairline of light along its top-left edge fading into a hairline of shadow along its bottom-right, the way light catches a pane. The slider is its strength; at zero there is none. **Rim color** is the colour of the lit edge, Automatic being a soft white on a dark theme and a brighter white on a light one, where the panes are pale and need the edge more. The shadowed edge is always a translucent black.

**Grain** lays a faint, fixed noise over each surface. A few percent is enough; it is what stops a large pane of glass from looking like flat plastic. The grain is the same tile on every surface and every launch, so a theme never twinkles.

## Liquid glass

**Kind of glass** has two settings. **Frosted** is everything above: the blurred slice under the surface's colour. **Liquid** is the look Apple calls liquid glass, and it changes what happens at the edge of every pane. Near the edge the backdrop is pulled inward, the way a thick lens magnifies what it covers, so the picture behind a key seems to bulge into it; red and blue part a little where it bends, like light through the edge of a prism; and a band of light sits along whichever edges face the light, from the upper left. The middle of each pane shows straight through, so a wide key is a lens and not a mirror. **Refraction** sets how far the edge bends the backdrop, **Color split** how far the colours part. The Liquid preset also drops the blur to almost nothing, turns the grain off and brightens the rim, since a lens is clear.

A lens needs two things. It needs a picture to bend, so it works over a background image or the wallpaper band and not over the blurred app, whose pixels belong to the system and cannot be read; a window-blur theme set to Liquid is a lens on a phone that cannot blur and frosted on one that can, unless **Behind the glass** says Wallpaper. And it needs Android 13 or later, where a pane can run a small pixel program; older phones draw a liquid theme as very clear frosted glass, with the same rim. The program runs on the graphics chip for the keys' pixels only, and it is recorded once per key, not re-run on every keystroke.

What is not here: Apple's panes also merge and stretch into each other as they move, and their highlight follows the phone's tilt. Neither is part of a theme yet.

## Presets and dressing a theme

The **Presets** row sets the glass sliders in one tap and makes the theme's fills see-through where they are not already:

| Preset | What it does |
|---|---|
| Frosted | Milky glass: a soft blur, colours lifted a little, a quiet rim. The default. |
| Clear | Nearly transparent panes with a bright rim, the way polished glass catches light. |
| Mica | Heavy blur and muted colour, like a wall of frosted acrylic. |
| Smoked | The backdrop dimmed, a low rim, a touch more grain. |
| Liquid | Thick clear lenses: the backdrop bent and colour-split at the edge, a bright rim, no grain. Android 13 and later draw the lens. |

A preset lowers the opacity of the letter-key, modifier-key, chip, tool and popup colours to what it needs, but only where a fill is still more opaque than that: a colour you have already made more see-through is left alone. It also gives the letter keys a [key gradient](/themes/editor/#gradients) sheen if the theme has none, so each pane catches the light across its top. Whether the app behind is blurred is left as you set it. Afterwards nothing remembers which preset was picked, and every slider still moves.

## The Frost family

Three built-in looks on one card, all glass:

- **Frost** blurs the app behind the keyboard. The board is a translucent navy tint over that blur, the keys panes of white at a fifth strength. On a phone that cannot blur, the board stands on your wallpaper band and the keys keep their rims. The tint is deliberately not lighter: over a white app, a thinner navy leaves white labels on pale grey.
- **Frost wallpaper** stands on your wallpaper outright and never blurs the app, so its backdrop is steady whatever you type into, and it is the look every phone and the gallery can show in full.
- **Frost light** is the same glass as Frost for a light phone.

## Details and edge cases

- **Contrast.** Glass is see-through by design, so what is behind it changes how readable the labels are. The Frost looks are checked against a white app and a black app, blurred and not; a theme of your own is yours to judge in the editor's preview, which has no app behind it and so shows the theme the way a phone that cannot blur draws it, on your wallpaper band.
- **The wallpaper band refreshes** when the wallpaper changes, when the theme is applied, and when the keyboard's size changes. It is one small picture in the same cache as the theme's background image.
- **High contrast** (under Accessibility) drops the glass with the rest of the decoration: the board goes solid and the keys with it.
- **Theme crossfade.** Switching themes eases the rim, the grain and the fallback opacity. The blur itself, its radius and the surface set switch over at the midpoint, since each would otherwise ask for a new bake or a new window layout on every frame of the fade.
- **The bars' held band.** The keyboard normally keeps a strip of empty window above the keys while a bar row such as the tools row is folded away, so toggling it never resizes the window. With the window blurred that strip would be a band of blurred app above the keys, so a glass theme gives the band up and takes the one resize instead.
- **Export.** A theme's glass settings travel in its `.wmtheme.json` file, the wallpaper choice included; the wallpaper itself is the other phone's own. An app version from before glass existed imports the same file as a plain translucent theme and loses nothing else.
